title: Properties, Records and Pattern Matching
summary: Write properties with validation, init-only and required members, declare immutable records with value equality, and match data with switch patterns.
introduction: Properties are how C# classes expose data without giving up control: they look like fields to callers but run code when read or written. Records build on properties to give you immutable data types with value equality in a single line. Pattern matching then lets you take decisions based on the shape of data (its type, its properties, a range) rather than long if chains. This lesson covers all three, which together define how modern C# models data.
learningObjectives: Write auto, computed, validated, init-only and required properties
Declare records and explain value equality and with expressions
Use type, relational, logical and property patterns in switch expressions

blocks.text: A **property** has a getter and optionally a setter. An *auto-property* (`{ get; set; }`) stores the value in a hidden field; a full property runs your code, which is where validation and normalisation go, and the `value` keyword inside a setter is the value being assigned. `init` instead of `set` allows assignment only while the object is being created, and `required` forces callers to set the property in an object initializer, so the compiler, not a runtime check, guarantees it is never missing.

rows: Set in the constructor or an object initializer, then frozen
Readable everywhere, writable only inside the class
Calculated on every read, nothing stored
The caller must set it when creating the object

blocks.text: A **record** is a type whose main job is to carry data. Declaring `record Point(int X, int Y)` generates, in one line, a constructor, two init-only properties, a readable `ToString`, **value equality** (`==` compares the properties, not the references), a matching `GetHashCode`, deconstruction into variables, and support for `with` expressions that copy an instance with some properties changed. Records are reference types by default; `record struct` gives a value type with the same conveniences. A record may also declare extra members in a body.

`with` did not touch `p1`; it produced a new record. Compare this with a class: two `new Point(3, 4)` class instances would be unequal under `==`, and you would have to write the constructor, properties, `Equals` and `ToString` yourself. Use records for values that are defined by their data: coordinates, money amounts, messages, objects read from JSON. Use classes for things with identity and changing state, such as a bank account.

You have already used `is` with a type and `switch` expressions with constants. Patterns combine: a **type pattern** (`int n`) tests the type and captures the value, a **relational pattern** (`< 0`) compares, `and`, `or` and `not` combine patterns, and `when` adds an arbitrary condition. Arms are tried in order, so put specific cases before general ones; here `0` must come before `int n`.

blocks.text: A **property pattern** matches on the values of properties, which is where records and pattern matching shine together. Combined with relational patterns it turns a set of business rules into a readable table, and the compiler warns if a later arm can never be reached.

blocks.title: with copies are shallow
blocks.text: `with` copies property values, so a record that contains a `List<T>` shares that list with its copy: changing the list through one record changes it for both, and the two records still compare equal only while they share the same list instance. Keep records immutable all the way down (use `ImmutableList<T>` or arrays you never mutate), or copy the collection yourself inside the `with` initializer.

questions.question: Two record instances with the same property values are equal under ==.
questions.explanation: Records implement value equality: `==`, `Equals` and `GetHashCode` all use the property values. Classes compare references unless you override equality yourself.

questions.question: Which pattern matches an int between 1 and 10 inclusive?
questions.explanation: Relational patterns are combined with `and`: `is >= 1 and <= 10`. The other forms are not C# syntax.
